titleEn: InsectBiotech Raises $8.3m to scale BSFL production in Andalusia, Spain
titleZh: InsectBiotech融资830万美元，利用黑水虻处理橄榄油废料
summaryZh: 西班牙初创公司InsectBiotech获得830万美元融资，将在安达卢西亚建设新工厂，利用黑水虻幼虫将橄榄油产业副产品转化为蛋白质、油脂和肥料。该公司采用低技术、中型规模、太阳能驱动的模式，解决了饲料和能源两大问题，计划到2027年投产，年产1300吨鲜幼虫，并已签署多份意向书。其创新点在于利用绿色化学处理橄榄果渣，使饲料成本降至传统配方的四分之一，并计划全球扩张。
featuredReason: 该新闻展示了昆虫蛋白生产与农业废弃物资源化的创新结合，为智慧畜牧行业提供了循环经济与降本增效的实践案例，值得关注其技术路径和商业模式。
contentFull:
Spanish startup InsectBiotech has raised €7.2 million ($8.3 million) to build a new facility in Andalusia using black soldier fly larvae to convert byproducts from the olive oil industry and other ag side streams into protein, oil, and fertilizer.

The round, which includes participation from Arcano Partners through the Impact Andalusía Innovation fund and undisclosed US investors, will support the construction of a site capable of processing up to 7,500 tons of agricultural by-products a year, said cofounder and COO Ben Brown.

The plant—which should be operational in Q3, 2027—”marks a significant step in the company’s transition from research and pilot operations to commercial-scale manufacturing,” said Brown. The site will produce 1,300 tons of fresh larvae per year, which translates to 300 tons of high protein meal. This will be followed by a ramp up to 10,000 tons of larvae.

“Close to a dozen LOIs (letters of intent) have been signed,” Brown told AgFunderNews. “The main off takers will be aquaculture, swine, poultry and pet food for protein; vineyards and high rotation crops (berries) for the frass; and biodiesel companies for the oil.”

Feedstock and energy

Formed by Tobias Webb, Ignacio Gavilan, and Ben Brown in 2022, InsectBiotech realized pretty quickly that the unit economics of farming black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) for protein, oil, and frass, only make sense if you can “solve two big problems: feedstock and energy,” said Webb.

“It hit Ben when he was driving through Andalucía [in southern Spain]. He rang me up and said, I’ve figured it out. There’s a huge amount of olive waste [pomace left over after olives are crushed for oil], and endless solar energy, giving us both feedstock and low energy costs in a region of Spain that really needs jobs, factories and investment.”

Brown added: “Olive oil production waste continues to be abundant throughout Spain. In standard seasons, processing actors (orujeras) collect the waste to extract residual pomace oil and use the dry cake for biomass, paying mills an amount per ton. There are approximately five million tons of waste every year, enough for several uses and users at a very reasonable cost. We have also further reduced supply risk by securing long-term agreements with processing plants to ensure reliable access over the long term.”

Olive pomace  

While several players at that time were arguing that the future of insect ag lay in vast, highly-automated—and very pricey—facilities that look like Amazon warehouses, Webb, Gavilan, and Brown started running the numbers and concluded that a lower-tech, medium-sized facility making 2,000+ tons of protein and 4,000 tons of frass (insect waste that can be used as a soil amendment) powered by renewable energy made the most sense for InsectBiotech.

“Andalucía produces the largest amount of olive pomace residue in the world in one place, but everyone we spoke to said we couldn’t use it as a feedstock. But we found a low-cost way of using green chemistry to make it digestible by removing anti-nutritional factors.”

According to Brown, the mechanical process is “highly economical, enabling feed costs of up to one-quarter those of conventional wheat-based formulations. As the technology is protected by an approved patent, it’s our secret sauce.” While the pomace has to be supplemented with some additional amino acids for balance, it accounts for 95% of the feedstock.

For energy, the plan is “to have 75-80% solar given the abundance of sunlight in southern Spain with more then 3,000 hours/year,” said Brown. “This will be supplemented with gas as needed.”

For neonates (infant BSF larvae) the aim is to “have a 50/50 split [of infants produced in-house and brought in from specialist hatcheries] to de-risk supply,” he said. “I think where this ends up is a bit like the poultry industry where you have rearing farms and people buy a few day-old chicks. I think genetics [of BSF for protein production] will also definitely get better.”

Second-generation insect ag

Stepping back, said Brown, players entering the insect ag space today benefit by being later to the game, as pioneers had to build the plane while flying it. The second wave of players can learn from their mistakes and work with firms that have built up specialist expertise in areas from breeding and genetics to infrastructure.

Today, he added, firms can buy off the shelf solutions from a number of different vendors.

“Our view is that the winning BSF farming model combines true agricultural waste as feedstock, low-opex EU production close to raw material sources, modular facility build-out, and hybrid technology that balances automation with skilled human resources, using efficient BSF production to deliver products that compete on cost, not sustainability alone.”

Commercially viable insect farming is not about a single breakthrough, but a complex of factors, said Brown. InsectBiotech’s model favors modular construction enabling capacity to be added gradually, cheap, abundant, pre-aggregated feedstocks, competitive labor costs and job creation in Just Transition zones, solar-powered operations, and “cost-competitive products aligned with mainstream demand versus premium pricing in niche markets.”

Longer term, he said, InsectBiotech aims to be a global player, utilizing olive pomace in several regions where olives are grown. “We’re not interested in having one small farm; we’re looking at a global stage. The plan is to have five farms in Spain, but potentially in Portugal and other olive pomace jurisdictions, which is about half dozen countries.”

translationZh:
西班牙初创公司InsectBiotech已筹集720万欧元（830万美元），将在安达卢西亚建设新工厂，利用黑水虻幼虫将橄榄油行业的副产品及其他农业侧流转化为蛋白质、油脂和肥料。

本轮融资包括Arcano Partners通过Impact Andalusía Innovation基金以及未披露的美国投资者的参与，将支持建设一座年处理能力达7500吨农业副产品的工厂，联合创始人兼首席运营官Ben Brown表示。

该工厂预计于2027年第三季度投入运营，"标志着公司从研发和中试运营向商业规模制造过渡的重要一步"，Brown说。该工厂将年产1300吨鲜幼虫，相当于300吨高蛋白粉。随后将扩大到10000吨幼虫。

"已签署近十几份意向书（LOI），"Brown告诉AgFunderNews。"主要承购方将是水产养殖、猪、禽和宠物食品的蛋白质；葡萄园和高轮作作物（浆果）的虫粪；以及生物柴油公司的油脂。"

**原料和能源**

InsectBiotech由Tobias Webb、Ignacio Gavilan和Ben Brown于2022年创立，他们很快意识到，养殖黑水虻幼虫（BSFL）用于蛋白质、油脂和虫粪的单位经济性，只有在你能够"解决两个大问题：原料和能源"时才成立，Webb说。

"Ben在开车穿过安达卢西亚（西班牙南部）时想到了这一点。他打电话给我说，我想明白了。这里有大量的橄榄废料（橄榄压榨油后剩下的果渣），还有无尽的太阳能，既提供了原料，又提供了低能源成本，而且这个西班牙地区确实需要就业、工厂和投资。"

Brown补充说："橄榄油生产废料在整个西班牙一直很丰富。在正常季节，加工商（orujeras）收集废料以提取剩余的果渣油，并将干饼用于生物质，每吨向榨油厂支付一定费用。每年大约有500万吨废料，足以供多种用途和用户使用，成本非常合理。我们还通过签订长期协议与加工厂确保长期可靠供应，进一步降低了供应风险。"

**橄榄果渣**

虽然当时有几家参与者认为昆虫农业的未来在于大型、高度自动化且非常昂贵的设施，看起来像亚马逊仓库，但Webb、Gavilan和Brown开始计算，并得出结论：一个技术含量较低、中型规模、年产2000多吨蛋白质和4000吨虫粪（可用作土壤改良剂的昆虫废料）的设施，由可再生能源驱动，对InsectBiotech来说最有意义。

"安达卢西亚是世界上最大的橄榄果渣残留物产地，但与我们交谈的每个人都说我们不能将其用作原料。但我们找到了一种低成本的方法，利用绿色化学去除抗营养因子，使其可消化。"

据Brown称，这种机械工艺"非常经济，饲料成本可低至传统小麦基配方的四分之一。由于该技术受已批准专利保护，这是我们的秘密武器。"虽然果渣需要补充一些额外的氨基酸以平衡营养，但它占原料的95%。

对于能源，计划是"75-80%的太阳能，因为西班牙南部阳光充足，每年超过3000小时"，Brown说。"这将根据需要辅以天然气。"

对于新生幼虫（幼龄黑水虻），目标是"50/50的比例（内部生产与从专业孵化场引进），以降低供应风险"，他说。"我认为这最终会有点像家禽业，有饲养场，人们购买几天大的雏鸡。我认为（用于蛋白质生产的黑水虻）遗传学也肯定会变得更好。"

**第二代昆虫农业**

退一步看，Brown说，今天进入昆虫农业领域的参与者受益于较晚进入，因为先驱者不得不在飞行中建造飞机。第二波参与者可以从他们的错误中学习，并与在育种、遗传学、基础设施等领域积累了专业知识的公司合作。

如今，他补充说，公司可以从多个不同供应商处购买现成解决方案。

"我们的观点是，成功的黑水虻养殖模式结合了真正的农业废料作为原料、靠近原料来源的低运营成本欧盟生产、模块化设施建设，以及平衡自动化与熟练人力资源的混合技术，利用高效的黑水虻生产提供在成本上具有竞争力的产品，而不仅仅是可持续性。"

商业上可行的昆虫养殖不是单一突破，而是多种因素的复杂组合，Brown说。InsectBiotech的模式倾向于模块化建设，使产能可以逐步增加；廉价、丰富、预聚集的原料；具有竞争力的劳动力成本和公正过渡区的就业创造；太阳能运营；以及"与主流需求一致的成本竞争力产品，而非小众市场的溢价定价。"

长期来看，他说，InsectBiotech的目标是成为全球参与者，在多个橄榄种植地区利用橄榄果渣。"我们不是只想要一个小农场；我们着眼于全球舞台。计划在西班牙建五个农场，但可能还会在葡萄牙和其他橄榄果渣产区，大约有六个国家。"
author: Elaine Watson
